cover.subtitle: A zero-knowledge end-to-end encrypted Texas Hold'em protocol — eliminate dealer cheating and build a trustless on-chain game economy.

abstract.label: Abstract
abstract.p1: ZGame is an end-to-end encrypted Texas Hold'em protocol built on zero-knowledge proofs. Traditional online poker depends on a centralized server for dealing, forcing players to trust the operator. ZGame solves this trust problem by implementing the Mental Poker protocol: every card is stored on-chain as an ElGamal ciphertext, and no single party (including the operator) can see another player's hand. All critical operations — shuffle, reveal, leave — are verified on-chain through six types of zero-knowledge proofs, achieving an end-to-end encrypted fair play experience.
abstract.p2: The system uses a three-layer architecture: a browser frontend, a Rust relay, and on-chain smart contracts. Cryptographically, it relies on the BLS12-381 curve and additively homomorphic ElGamal encryption, with support for dynamic player join, leave, and deck reconstruction. The economic model uses real on-chain tokens, with sponsored transactions delivering a zero-Gas experience.
abstract.p3: ZGame's long-term ambition goes well beyond poker. The project plans to build a Layer 1 blockchain purpose-built for game scenarios, with custom transaction ordering and a fully gasless business model, and to explore zero-knowledge virtual machines for the ultimate on-chain game experience. In the end, ZGame aims to build a trustless game economy that spans every genre of on-chain gaming — making cryptographic security the base layer of all on-chain games.

s1.title: The Trust Crisis of Centralized Online Poker
s1.p1: Online poker is a multi-billion-dollar industry, but its core mechanics — dealing and shuffling — have always relied on a centralized server. Players cannot verify that the server deals fairly; the operator has full cheating power: it can see every hand, manipulate the dealing order, and leak information to specific players. Multiple historical scandals have proven that this trust model is fragile.
s1.mark: Before the cards are dealt, no party should be able to predict any face-down card.

s2.title: The Blockchain Game Dilemma
s2.p1: Moving games on-chain solves transparency but creates a new challenge. Fully on-chain dealing exposes every card to the whole network, breaking the information asymmetry that is essential to poker. Going back to off-chain dealing returns to the centralized trust model. The core technical challenge of on-chain poker is finding a balance between transparency and confidentiality.
s2.p2: On top of that, Web3 games face user-experience barriers: wallet management, Gas fees, and transaction confirmation delays make ordinary players walk away. A sustainable on-chain poker protocol must find the optimal point across cryptographic security, on-chain auditability, and user experience.

s3.title: The Limits of General-Purpose Chains
s3.p1: Today's general-purpose blockchains are not designed for game scenarios. In high-frequency interactive games, the throughput, confirmation latency, and ordering model of general chains cannot meet real-time requirements. Game actions must compete with NFT mints and DeFi protocols for block space, so during volatile periods the network congests and the experience degrades. Games don't need a chain that 'can run contracts' — they need a chain 'born for games.' That is the ultimate direction of ZGame.

s1.title: Mental Poker: Forty Years from Theory to Engineering
s1.p1: In 1981, Shamir, Rivest, and Adleman posed the Mental Poker problem: can two mutually distrustful parties play poker over the phone while each is sure the other isn't cheating? The cryptographic solution — later known collectively as the Mental Poker protocol — is the theoretical cornerstone of ZGame.
s1.mark: It is the recent breakthroughs in zero-knowledge proofs that turned Mental Poker from an academic toy into an engineering scheme that can run in real-time online environments. ZGame is born at exactly that inflection point.

s2.title: The Core Insight
s2.p1: ZGame's central design idea is simple: the deck is always kept encrypted, dealing is just distributing ciphertext indices, and revealing requires cooperative decryption by all players. No single entity — not even the operating server — can decrypt independently. This property eliminates dealing-side cheating at the cryptographic root.
s2.mark: The deck is always encrypted; dealing is just distributing ciphertext indices; revealing requires cooperative decryption by all players.

s3.title: Core Innovation: Dynamic Player Departure and Deck Reconstruction
s3.p1: Classical Mental Poker has a long-ignored fatal flaw: it assumes all participants stay online for the entire hand. As soon as any player leaves, their private key is permanently missing from the aggregated public key, and the encrypted deck can no longer be decrypted — the hand must terminate. In real online poker, players leaving mid-game due to network issues, voluntary exit, or ejection is the norm. This means classical Mental Poker is almost unusable in practice.

l1.title: Ciphertext Layer Stripping
l1.desc: The departing player submits a LeaveProof (DLEq zero-knowledge proof) showing they correctly removed their own encryption layer, without leaking any card information.

l2.title: Aggregated Public Key Update
l2.desc: The aggregated public key subtracts the leaver's public key; the remaining players' key combination can still decrypt the deck.

l3.title: Ejection and Reconstruction
l3.desc: If a player is kicked out for timeout or misbehavior, the system gathers the readable cards (partially-decrypted ciphertext) from the rest, runs a four-layer ReconstructProof, and securely swaps the ejected player's cards out of the deck, re-encrypting the whole deck with fresh randomness.

l4.title: Seamless Continuation
l4.desc: Once reconstruction completes, the remaining players continue the hand on the updated deck — no need to restart. Newcomers' hole cards are unaffected, and the community cards remain consistent.

s3.conclusion: Players can join and leave at any time, and a hand is never forced to abort due to roster changes. This is ZGame's core innovation over every prior Mental Poker implementation, and the key step that takes the classic protocol from the lab to production.

s4.title: System Architecture Overview
s4.p1: ZGame currently uses a three-layer architecture:

c1.title: Frontend
c1.desc: React + Vite + TypeScript. All encryption and ZK proof generation runs locally via WebAssembly. Real-time updates over WebSocket.

c2.title: Relay Layer
c2.desc: Rust + Axum + WebSocket. On-chain event listening, transaction construction and sponsorship, real-time broadcast, timeout and retry management.

c3.title: On-Chain Layer
c3.desc: Smart contracts handle shared-object state management, on-chain verification of the six ZK proofs, betting logic, and fund settlement.

s1.title: Card Representation and Key System
s1.p1: The system uses the BLS12-381 G1 group as the cryptographic foundation. The 52 playing cards are mapped to 52 deterministic G1 points via standard hash-to-curve:
s1.p2: Each player generates a private key sk and a public key pk = G * sk. All players' public keys are summed to form the Aggregated Public Key AggPK = sum(pk_i). Only the joint possession of all private keys can decrypt the ciphertext.

s2.title: ElGamal Encryption and Shuffling
s2.p1: The deck is stored as ElGamal ciphertext, 96 bytes per card (c1: 48 bytes + c2: 48 bytes). The initial deck is plaintext-encrypted under the identity key, i.e. c1 = G, c2 = plaintext_i.

l1.title: Permute
l1.desc: Randomly permute the order of the 52 cards.

l2.title: Re-encrypt
l2.desc: Add a fresh encryption layer over each card under the aggregated public key with new random masks.

s2.p2: After each shuffle, the player submits a ShuffleProof showing the output deck is a valid permutation-plus-re-encryption of the input deck, without leaking the permutation. After every player has shuffled in turn, the plaintext content, order, and player-to-card mapping of the deck is hidden cryptographically.

s3.title: Distributed Reveal
s3.p1: When dealing, ciphertexts are taken from the shuffled deck in order and assigned to hole cards or the community pool. Each card is still ciphertext, and distributed decryption is required to recover plaintext.
s3.p2: For a ciphertext CT = (c1, c2), player i computes their own Reveal Token:
s3.p3: Summing all tokens gives sum(token_i) = c1 * sum(sk_i); the plaintext is then c2 - sum(token_i). Each submission is accompanied by a Chaum-Pedersen DLEq proof showing log_G(pk_i) == log_c1(token_i), preventing fake tokens that would corrupt the revealed card.

s4.title: Dynamic Player Management
s4.p1: Real games require support for mid-hand join and leave. ZGame defines a complete dynamic player protocol:

l1.title: Join
l1.desc: A new player first remasks the current deck (c2 += c1 * sk) with their private key, then shuffles. Requires RemaskProof + ShuffleProof.

l2.title: Leave
l2.desc: A player removes their own encryption layer (c2 -= c1 * sk) and submits LeaveProof; the aggregated public key subtracts their public key.

l3.title: Reconstruct
l3.desc: If a player is kicked or times out, the remaining players collaboratively swap the leaver's cards out of the deck, re-encrypt the whole deck with fresh randomness, and submit ReconstructProof. Once reconstruction completes, all remaining players reshuffle, ensuring the leaver's private key plays no part in any future round.

intro.tail: are used across the system. All are based on the Fiat-Shamir heuristic with a SHA3-256 transcript, ensuring that the Rust-side proof generation and the on-chain contract verification stay in lockstep.

p1.title: PK Ownership Proof (Schnorr)
p1.desc: At registration, a player proves they hold the private key for their public key, preventing malicious injection of invalid keys. Standard Schnorr: commitment = G * omega, challenge = H(G || pk || commitment), response = omega + challenge * sk.

p2.title: Shuffle Proof (ZKShuffleProof)
p2.desc: Proves the output deck is a valid permutation-plus-re-encryption of the input deck. A three-layer Schnorr design: combined proof + c1-only proof + c2-only proof, preventing information-shift (c1/c2 swap) attacks.

p3.title: Remask Proof (DLEqProof)
p3.desc: On join, proves the player correctly added their encryption layer. Verifies output.c2 - input.c2 = input.c1 * sk, with each card independently bound.

p4.title: Leave Proof (DLEqProof)
p4.desc: On leave, proves the player correctly removed their encryption layer. Symmetric to RemaskProof, verifies c2' = c2 - c1 * sk.

p5.title: Reveal Token Proof (Chaum-Pedersen DLEq)
p5.desc: When submitting a Reveal Token, proves token = c1 * sk and pk = G * sk. A double discrete-log equality proof, with an anti-replay nonce to prevent replay attacks.

p6.title: Reconstruct Proof (Composite)
p6.desc: Used after ejecting a player. The most complex proof in the system, with four layers: SwapOutCardProof (Chaum-Pedersen DLEq), Blind DLEq Proof, Generalized Schnorr Proof, and Total DLEq Proof.

security.title: Security Hardening
security.l1: M-D13 / c1-c2 swap attack: ShuffleProof adds independent c1 / c2 Schnorr proofs.
security.l2: M4 / Reveal Token replay: nonce introduced and bound to expected_pk.
security.l3: M-P17 / Identity commitment attack: all proofs reject identity points as commitments or ciphertexts.
security.l4: M7 / Identity c1 attack: remask_ciphertext and leave_ciphertext reject c1 == identity.
security.l5: M6 / Zero private key attack: player registration and proof verification reject pk == identity.

ch5.title: 05 Complete Game Flow
ch5.p1: The following stages are executed synchronously between the off-chain Rust service and the on-chain smart contract. All critical cryptographic operations run locally in the user's device:

r3.c2: Every active player shuffles in turn

r5.c2: Submit Reveal Token for other players' hands

r8.c2: Submit Reveal Token for community cards
r8.c3: Plaintext published on-chain after all tokens collected

r10.c2: Non-folded players reveal own hole cards

timeout.title: Timeout and Fault Tolerance
timeout.l1: Shuffle timeout: kick the current shuffler, rebuild the deck, and the remaining players reshuffle.
timeout.l2: Reveal timeout: kick players who did not submit tokens. In Pre-Flop, restart the hand; later stages trigger Reconstruct.

s1.title: Token Redemption and Chip System
s1.p1: In-game chips are pegged to the chain's native token at a fixed ratio. When sitting down, players deposit tokens; the smart contract converts the amount into stack and credits the seat. At hand end, stack is converted back to tokens at the same ratio and refunded directly to the player. All in-game betting, blinds, and side pots are denominated in stack.

s2.title: Side Pot Computation
s2.p1: When a player goes all-in, the system automatically computes side pots. The algorithm:
s2.l1: Find all all-in players (bet > 0 and stack == 0).
s2.l3: For each all-in player, compute other players' excess over that bet; move the excess from the main pot to a new side pot.
s2.l4: The side pot's eligible list is all non-folded players who contributed to the excess.

s3.title: Zero-Gas Experience
s3.p1: Through sponsored transactions, ZGame delivers a zero-Gas game experience. Players do not need to hold any native token for Gas; all Gas is paid by the protocol. Wallet-based sign-in keeps the Web3 onboarding friction low.

s1.title: 7.1 Card Secrecy
s1.p1: The deck is always under multiple layers of ElGamal encryption. Decrypting a single card requires the joint private keys of every participant. No single player, server, or external observer can independently decrypt any face-down card. This property is guaranteed by the BLS12-381 discrete-log hardness.

s2.title: 7.2 Shuffle Integrity
s2.p1: ShuffleProof guarantees that each player's shuffle is an honest permutation-plus-re-encryption — no one can secretly swap, drop, or duplicate cards. The initial deck is a deterministic set of 52 G1 points, ruling out 'custom deck' attacks.

s3.title: 7.3 Dealing and Reveal Verifiability
s3.p1: Dealing takes cards in order from the verified encrypted deck, fully public and auditable. Each Reveal submits a RevealTokenProof, and only after on-chain verification is the partial decryption accepted.

s4.title: 7.4 Dynamic Membership Security
s4.p1: RemaskProof / LeaveProof guarantees that on join or leave, the deck's encryption layer is correctly added or removed. ReconstructProof ensures that after a player is kicked, the leaver's private key can decrypt nothing further.

s5.title: 7.5 Anti-Sybil and Identity Binding
s5.p1: PKOwnershipProof forces every player to prove they hold the private key for their public key. The public key is bound to the seat and the on-chain address, preventing a single entity from faking multiple identities to manipulate the game.

s6.title: 7.6 On-Chain Auditability
s6.p1: All critical cryptographic operations can be submitted to the on-chain contract for verification. State snapshots provide a complete encrypted-state record that any client can independently validate for deck consistency.

c1.title: Cryptographic Security
c1.l1: End-to-end encryption — the server never sees plaintext cards.
c1.l2: Six zero-knowledge proofs cover every critical operation.
c1.l4: Dynamic player management, support for mid-hand join and leave.

c2.title: User Experience
c2.l3: WebAssembly local compute, zero-latency crypto operations.
c2.l4: WebSocket real-time communication for smooth play.

c3.title: On-Chain Transparency
c3.l1: All critical operations are verifiable on-chain.
c3.l2: Complete encrypted state snapshots, public and queryable.
c3.l4: Open-source contracts and proof verification logic.

c4.title: Fault Tolerance and Liveness
c4.l1: Per-stage timeout prevents games from hanging.
c4.l2: Auto-rebuild on disconnect, no game interruption.
c4.l3: Off-chain timeout handling + on-chain state sync.
c4.l4: New players can join without restarting a hand.

r4.c4: On-chain event listener, tx builder, real-time broadcast

r6.c4: Contract byte format and Rust type conversion

r8.c4: Table main logic, state machine, settlement

ch10.title: 10 Custom L1: A Blockchain Born for Games

s1.title: The Bottleneck of General-Purpose Chains
s1.p1: ZGame's current MVP runs on an existing general-purpose chain, validating the core cryptographic protocol. But as the product matures, fundamental limits surface: game actions share block space and ordering priority with every other app on the chain, leading to unpredictable confirmation latency, volatile Gas fees, and broken high-frequency interaction. General-purpose chains are designed to 'do everything' — games need to 'do one thing to the extreme.'

s2.title: The Hyperliquid Lesson
s2.p1: Hyperliquid provides the strongest practical sample of the application-specific-chain pattern. As a Layer 1 purpose-built for derivatives trading, Hyperliquid is not built on top of any general chain — it builds its own consensus, execution, and ordering rules from scratch. This design delivers three core advantages:

l1.title: On-chain order book + in-memory matching
l1.desc: All placements, cancels, and fills happen directly on-chain; order matching runs in memory, with throughput over 20,000 TPS.

l2.title: Zero Gas + table-fee revenue
l2.desc: Users pay no Gas; protocol revenue comes from trading fees. Validators earn from protocol inflation rewards and fee sharing, forming a flywheel: more volume → more revenue → more security.

l3.title: Fully verifiable state
l3.desc: The complete state, including the order book, is publicly auditable to all validators while keeping a CEX-grade user experience.

s2.p2: By late 2025, Hyperliquid had captured over 40% of the major Layer 1 blockchain fee market, proving that the application-specific-chain path is not only technically viable but also commercially self-consistent.

s3.title: ZGame L1 Design Direction
s3.p1: ZGame plans to build a Layer 1 blockchain purpose-built for on-chain games, borrowing Hyperliquid's core philosophy but moving the target scenario from derivatives trading to real-time competitive games. The core design principles:

c1.title: Custom Ordering
c1.desc: Game actions are ordered by game-logic rules rather than Gas bidding. The execution order of bets, reveals, and folds is determined by the game state machine, preventing MEV front-running and ordering manipulation.

c2.title: Fully Gasless
c2.desc: Users pay no Gas. Protocol revenue comes from table fees (a fixed percentage per hand). Validators earn from fee sharing and protocol inflation.

c3.title: In-Memory State Machine
c3.desc: High-frequency game actions execute in memory and are batched to the chain for final settlement. Players experience latency on par with traditional online games, not the seconds-long confirmation of typical chains.

s4.title: Business Model Comparison
s4.conclusion: The core logic of this business model is: more players → more active tables → more table-fee revenue → better validator earnings → stronger network security → better player experience. It is a fully self-consistent positive flywheel, in the same spirit as Hyperliquid's success in derivatives trading.

ch11.title: 11 Zero-Knowledge Virtual Machine: The Ultimate On-Chain Game Experience

s1.title: The Computation Challenge for Game State
s1.p1: Even on a custom L1, traditional blockchain verification still faces a fundamental conflict: the per-node cost of verifying each transaction on-chain limits the complexity of any single transaction. ZGame's cryptographic proofs (especially ShuffleProof's 52-card permutation verification) already sit at the upper bound of per-tx compute. More complex game genres — real-time strategy, open-world exploration, physics simulation — have state compute requirements that far exceed the limit of on-chain execution today.

s2.title: Hypernova: A Continuously-Running Zero-Knowledge VM
s2.p1: ZGame is exploring the Hypernova frontier — building a continuously-running zero-knowledge virtual machine (Succinct Zero-Knowledge VM). The core ideas:

l1.title: Off-chain execution, on-chain proof
l1.desc: Game logic runs in a high-performance off-chain environment (similar to traditional game servers) and periodically emits a ZK proof that all state transitions since the last proof point are valid. The chain only verifies one succinct proof, rather than re-executing every operation.

l2.title: Incremental Proofs
l2.desc: Using incremental verifiable compute, each proof only needs to cover the newly added computation, not start from scratch. This lets a continuously running game state efficiently emit cumulative proofs.

l3.title: Sub-second response
l3.desc: Because the chain only checks a proof (not every operation), player confirmation latency drops to sub-second, matching the experience of traditional online games.

s3.title: What This Means for ZGame
s3.p1: Hypernova extends ZGame's reach from 'Texas Hold'em' to any on-chain game scenario:

c1.title: Unbounded Computation
c1.desc: Regardless of game complexity, on-chain verification cost is constant. Supports physics engines, AI decisions, large-world generation, and other compute-intensive games.

c2.title: Privacy Extension
c2.desc: ZK proofs not only verify operation legality but also hide game-state details (e.g., hand cards in card games, troop deployments in strategy games).

c3.title: Cross-game Composition
c3.desc: Multiple games share the same ZK VM, enabling cross-game trustworthy transfer of assets and state, building a unified base layer for on-chain game economies.

ch12.title: 12 The Vision: A Trustless On-Chain Game Economy

intro.mark: We are building the infrastructure layer for the entire on-chain game industry
intro.tail: — a trustless game economy based on zero-knowledge proofs.

s1.title: From Poker to Multi-Genre Games
s1.p1: ZGame's Mental Poker protocol is an instance of a broader 'Mental Game' pattern. Its core cryptographic primitives — encrypted state, distributed decryption, verifiable state transition — can be directly ported to other game genres:

l1.title: Card Games
l1.desc: TCG, Hearthstone-style battles, UNO and more can all reuse the encrypted-deck and reveal-token protocol.

l2.title: Board Games
l2.desc: Go, chess and other board games face the 'public state exposes your strategy' problem on chain; ZK proofs can hide intermediate moves and only publish the full game record at the end.

l3.title: Tabletop & Social Deduction
l3.desc: Mafia, Avalon and similar games need a balance between 'hidden information' and 'verifiable fairness' — ZGame's cryptographic foundation applies directly.

l4.title: MMO and Open World
l4.desc: Powered by the Hypernova ZK VM, real-time open-world games can run complex state safely on-chain, achieving true asset ownership and a verifiable economy.

s2.title: The Trustless Economy
s2.p1: Traditional on-chain games suffer one fundamental problem: players cannot trust that the operator won't manipulate drop rates, economic parameters, or asset issuance in the dark. ZGame's cryptographic scheme gives the entire on-chain game industry a verifiable trust foundation:

v1.title: Core Principle: Verifiable Fairness
v1.desc: Every random event, every state transition, and every asset flow in a game can be verified on-chain via ZK proofs. Operators cannot manipulate results in the dark, and players don't need to trust anyone.

v2.title: Core Principle: Asset Sovereignty
v2.desc: In-game assets — chips, items, characters, land — exist as on-chain tokens, giving players true ownership. No matter how the operator changes, players' assets remain safe.

v3.title: Core Principle: Cross-game Interoperability
v3.desc: All games on the custom L1 share a unified economic layer and identity layer. Assets earned in one game can be used in another, building a true on-chain game metaverse economy.

p1.title: Phase 1: MVP (Completed)
p1.desc: Core Mental Poker protocol implementation, 6 ZK proofs, complete Texas Hold'em flow, social-account sign-in, zero-Gas experience.

p2.title: Phase 2: On-Chain Verification Hardening
p2.desc: Migrate ZK proof verification from off-chain pre-verification to on-chain contract verification, achieving a fully trustless-against-relayer security model.

p3.title: Phase 3: Multi-Genre Game Expansion
p3.desc: Extend the Mental Game protocol to other poker variants (Omaha, Stud) and encrypted card-game genres, validating protocol generality.

p4.title: Phase 4: Custom Game L1
p4.desc: Build a Layer 1 purpose-built for game scenarios, achieving custom ordering, fully zero-Gas, and the table-fee business model, eliminating general-chain performance bottlenecks.

p5.title: Phase 5: Zero-Knowledge Virtual Machine
p5.desc: Integrate the Hypernova ZK VM, realizing the off-chain-execution + on-chain-proof compute paradigm, supporting arbitrary-complexity on-chain games, with sub-second confirmation latency.

p6.title: Phase 6: Game Economic Ecosystem
p6.desc: Open the custom L1 and ZK VM to third-party game developers, building a trustless game economy spanning every genre. Achieve cross-game asset interoperability and a unified identity layer.

p7.title: Phase 7: Decentralized Governance
p7.desc: Introduce DAO governance, with community-driven protocol upgrades, parameter adjustments, and table-fee distribution, achieving a fully decentralized game protocol.

ch13.title: 13 Conclusion

intro.mark: No party can predict any face-down card before the deal.
intro.tail: ZGame shows a real-world application of frontier cryptography in blockchain gaming. Through BLS12-381 ElGamal encryption, six zero-knowledge proofs, and a distributed decryption protocol, ZGame achieves a security guarantee in a fully decentralized environment that traditional online poker never could.

ch13.p2: But ZGame's ambition does not end there. With a custom L1 dedicated to game scenarios and a ZK virtual machine that breaks the on-chain compute ceiling, ZGame is evolving from a poker game into the infrastructure layer for the entire on-chain game industry. On top of this infrastructure, game developers can build any type of on-chain game, players can truly own their assets, and operators can no longer manipulate results in the dark.
ch13.p3: Hyperliquid proved the feasibility and commercial self-consistency of the 'application-specific chain + table-fee model' in derivatives trading. ZGame brings this paradigm to gaming and goes further by satisfying gaming's unique information-asymmetry needs through zero-knowledge proofs. When games no longer require players to trust anyone, and assets are no longer subject to any centralized server, on-chain games will truly become the next trillion-dollar Web3 vertical.
